english: Snow lay on the field. Holding his daughter, the father sat by the fire and said: "A daughter has been born to me in winter. Your mother toiled (in labor) in the night. O Fire, hear me, you who protect us. Now I have given my daughter a famous name. Daughter, may you grow up in my home, and may you be dear to your husband. May you have plenty of wool; may the cold not seize you; may the fire warm you; may sons be born to you, and may daughters be born to you." So he spoke, and the fire burned.
uncertain: ḱémh₂t: 'became tired / toiled'; read as labor of childbirth
ḱóymoy: loc. of adj. ḱóymos 'homely, of the family', used substantivally 'in (my) home'
h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂ toy pl̥h₁éwih₂ h₁syéh₁t: lit. 'may wool be plentiful for you'
nu mléwHt: PST 'he was speaking'; taken as closing formula 'so he spoke'

english: The old man lay (dying), and his breath was leaving him. His children stood around him. He said: "Listen to me. I am thirsty; bring me water. I am going to the fathers. Guard the herd together, and do not strike your brother. Give me poured mead; cover me with earth and set up a stone. Remember my name." Then he spoke no more, and they wept.
uncertain: h₂éǵmn̥: 'army, flock, crowd'; here herd/flock
ph₂térn̥s h₁éymi: acc. pl. of goal, 'I go to the fathers' (= the ancestors, i.e. I am dying)
ḱóm: taken as adverb 'together'; also deictic acc. 'this one'
h₂ew ne bʰéh₂t: h₂ew 'away/again' + ne read as 'no longer spoke'
misfit: téwe: 2sg 'your (sg.)' inside commands addressed to several people (ph₂sté, stundté, 2pl); 'each of you, your brother' is a possible reading, but the expected form is plural (wos / yusmé-)

english: The master was driving the herd to the field in winter. Snow came, and he did not come back. His wife sat and watched the path. Wolves howled in the night. At dawn she found him: snow lay on him, the cold had seized him, he was dead. She became a widow and wept. Her husband's brother arrived. He said: "Woman, do not weep. I will nourish your child and guard your field." Then the widow spoke: "You are good, and I will live in your home." The widow lived in his home.
uncertain: h₂éǵmn̥ h₂éǵrom: two accusatives; read as object (herd) + goal (to the field)
h₂ew-kʷe ne gʷémt: no subject given; read as 'he (the master) did not come back'; if snígʷʰs carries over: 'and (the snow) did not go away'
h₁ésmi: loc. 'on him', not 1sg 'I am'
h₁widʰéwh₂ (subject of wérh₁t, tḱéyt): analyzer gives VOC/LEMMA; taken as nom. sg.
misfit: h₁widʰéwh₂n̥s: acc. pl. 'widows' as predicate of bʰúHt 'she became'; a nom. sg. (h₁widʰéwh₂) is needed

english: The sheep said to the horses: "My heart pains me, seeing a man driving horses."
uncertain: whole text: Schleicher-fable style without laryngeals or accents (owis, eḱwobʰyos, eweket, aǵontm̥); analyzer cannot parse most tokens; translated from the forms themselves
angʰetai: middle 'is constricted' = 'aches, pains'
widontei: dat. sg. ptcp. agreeing with moi 'to me, seeing'

english: The warrior lay down and spoke to his sons: "I was a warrior. I slew the serpent, and I slew the king's enemies. I drove the king's chariot. My fame is great. Now death is coming to me, and I am not afraid. Mortals die; gods do not die. If a mortal's name lives, his fame is imperishable. Let your fame be great." Then his breath left him.
uncertain: sékʷt: two homographs 'followed' / 'said'; with dat. suHnúbʰos read as 'said to his sons'
gʷʰénm̥: PST (imperfect) 'I was slaying / used to slay'; rendered 'I slew'
gʰóstins: 'guests / strangers / enemies'; enemies fits
h₁yód: 'if/when'

english: The daughter came to her father, and he said to her: "A man has come to us; he seeks you. Will you go to him?" The daughter said: "I will go, and I fear the strangers' house." Then her mother said to her: "Do not tremble. When I came to the household, I too was afraid. I have seen the man, and he is good. His house is bright and his horses are swift." Then the daughter stood up and went to her mother.
uncertain: h₂éǵt: no subject given; the speaker must be the father, so the subject switches from the daughter
ḱóm: 'with/together' or deictic acc.; meaning in h₁yód ḱóm ḱóymom h₁ludʰóm unclear ('when I came into the household together = married'?)
dʰéh₁mn̥: 'that which is set down; building'; rendered 'house'
h₁ésyeh₂s ph₂térm̥: anaphoric 'her', not reflexive; taken as the daughter's own father
misfit: h₁ésmi: 1sg 'I am' (or loc. 'on him') where 3pl h₁sénti 'are' is needed with the subject h₁éḱwōs HéHḱewes 'horses swift'

english: The widow came to the king. The queen sat beside the king. The widow spoke: "O king, I am a widow, and my husband is dead. My husband's brothers are seizing my field. Protect me and my child." The king looked at the widow and spoke to them (the brothers): "Whose is it?" They said: "It is ours." The king said: "It belongs to the widow's child. Give it back, and give the widow ten sheep." They obeyed the king and gave it back.
uncertain: h₁éy: anaphoric nom. sg. m. 'it', referring to the field (h₂éǵros, masc.)
tóybʰos: dat. pl. 'to those'; referent (the brothers) not named in that sentence
méne me ǵónh₁om-kʷe: méne 'my' goes with ǵónh₁om; word order unusual
h₂ew dédh₃te / h₂ew dh₃ént: h₂ew 'away/again' read as 'give back'
ḱluwént: AOR 'heard'; rendered 'obeyed'

english: Their father was dead. The three brothers sat down. The one who drives the horses said: "The horses are mine." The one who ploughs said: "Give me two horses." "Those two I will not give." Then one brother struck the other, and the other struck him. (The horses) fled and ran to the river. The river carried a horse away. Then they saw it in the water and were afraid. The one who herds the sheep cried out: "What are you two doing?"
uncertain: tóh₁ mē h₁opéyōh₂: mē with SBJV 1sg is literally 'let me not give'; a refusal 'I will not give' would more usually take ne
tóh₁ mē h₁opéyōh₂: speaker not named; taken as the horse-driver
bʰugént ... dr̥mént: no subject given; taken as the horses (also possible: the brothers)
dʰedʰh₁th₁és: PRS 2du 'are you two doing'; context suggests 'what have you done'

english: At dawn the brothers carried the dead man out of the house. They dressed him in a robe. A crowd followed him. They laid him on wood and carried fire around him. The fire burned him, and the smoke went up to the sky. His wife wept, and the dog howled. Then they covered him with earth. They set up a stone above him and gave poured mead to the dead man. The sun set. Then night came, and the dog lay down by the stone.
uncertain: pĺ̥h₂seh₂h₁: lexicon glosses 'a type of women's garment'; odd for a dead man; also could be acc. du. 'two garments'
dréwi: loc. of dóru 'tree'; read as 'on the wood (pyre)'
bʰoréyont: iterative 'carried around'; object péh₂wr̥ 'fire'
HréwdHt (dog): 'cry out' = 'howled'

english: The sister was sitting on the stone. Her brother arrived and said to her: "Our father is dead. Now who will guard the cattle?" He said: "I will protect them. Who will nourish our mother? I will nourish her." Then he said: "What will you do, sister?" She said: "I will guard the fire and remember his words." Then the dog came and lay down between them.
uncertain: wéwket / sékʷt: no subjects; read as the brother continuing to speak; the sister could be the one saying 'I will protect them', but then the question 'what will you do, sister?' makes less sense
h₂léksoh₂ / h₂éloh₂: PRS 1sg, rendered as future intent
misfit: h₁ésmey: masc./neut. dat. 'to him/it', but the person addressed is the sister; a fem. dat. h₁ésyeh₂ey is needed

english: A great bull was leading the herd, and an old bull went with him. The great bull said to him: "You are old. Go away from us." He went away. The sun burned and the river dried up. The herd was thirsty. The great bull found no water. The other one stood on a rock. He said: "I know (where there is) water. It is under the rock." He led them to it, and they drank and were satisfied. Strength belongs to the great bull; the old bull knows the way.
uncertain: h₂nḗr: 'man' or 'power, vital force'; the moral needs 'strength'
h₂élyos: 'the other', i.e. the old bull
tr̥pént: homographs 'were sated' / 'turned'; 'were sated' fits
wódr̥ wóydh₂e: lit. 'I know water'

english: The old man was sitting. The snow was melting, and the river filled up. The daughter-in-law came to him and said: "Father-in-law, a son has been born to me." The old man looked at him (the child), rejoiced, and said: "I am old and I shall die, but my name will not die. I have given my name to my grandson; he will carry it forward. Mortals die; a famous name lives."
uncertain: h₁ím (after ǵérh₂onts): masc. 'him'; read as the newborn son
h₁éy: anaphoric nom. sg. m. 'he' (the grandson)
méroh₂ / méreti: SBJV, rendered as future

english: O husband, you have gone away. Who will guard the sheep, who will plough? Now I am a widow; my heart has grown cold. The fire burns, but you do not sit by it. I look at your place: where are you? I watch the path. Husband, come back! Your children are weeping. The dog is looking for you. I cooked for you, and you do not eat. Now the earth covers you.
uncertain: h₁ésmi-ge: loc. 'by it (the fire)' + emphatic -ge, not 1sg 'I am'
pékʷom: PST 1sg 'I was cooking'; rendered 'I cooked'
sth₂dʰlóm: 'place, position, stall'; 'your place (seat)'

english: The father stood in front of the wagon and said to his daughter: "Daughter, you are going from my house to your husband's house. Listen to your parents-in-law and guard his fire. Do not deceive your husband; be dear to his brother. Take wool, a robe and a fleece. Remember your mother. Nourish your child. May the gods make your path straight. If distress comes to you, come to us. Our house stands (open) for you. Daughter, go."
uncertain: swéḱuroybʰos: dat. pl. of 'father-in-law'; rendered 'parents-in-law'
h₁ésyo péh₂wr̥: masc. 'his fire'; referent taken as the husband
h₁ésyo dʰugh₂tréy (opening): anaphoric 'his', not reflexive; taken as the father's own daughter
moysóm: 'ram; fleece'; fleece fits among gifts of wool/garment
h₁áyso: MID IMP 'receive, take'

english: Whoever supports the old father, the old man's house shall be his. Whoever abandons the old father, nothing of the herd shall be his. If a man has no son, his daughter's son shall take the field. If he has no grandson, his brother shall take it. Let the widow keep the field for her child. No one shall take it.
uncertain: h₂élēti: 'nourishes'; rendered 'supports'
kʷid ... mē h₁ést: indefinite with prohibitive mē + injunctive, 'let nothing be his'
h₁yód: 'if'
h₁ím kʷis ne h₁áyetor: kʷis ne 'no one'; the field is 'it' (h₁ím, masc.)

english: The father lay (dying), and those three sat by him. A son spoke: "To whom are you giving the house?" The old man said: "I give it to the one who nourishes me." Another said: "I bring you water." (Another:) "I milk the cows for you." The old man looked at their work and pointed to the middle one. The middle one said: "I did not nourish you for the sake of the house." (The father:) "The house is yours."
uncertain: tréyes-kʷe tóy h₁ésmi: 'those three' (the sons) sat 'by him' (loc. h₁ésmi)
gʷṓs toy h₂mélǵmi: no speaker given; taken as a third son
démey: dat. of dṓm; read as dative of purpose 'for (the sake of) the house'; a loc. démi 'in the house' would give a different sense
dṓm toy h₁ésti: no speaker given; taken as the father's verdict
h₃épos: 'work'; tóysōm 'their'

english: Dawn shone. The master's daughter came out, and her mother wept and dressed her in a woollen robe. The robe was red. The men yoked the cattle to the wagon. The wagon was the carpenter's work, and the yoke was the smith's work. Her husband lifted her up onto it, and her brother followed her. The wheel of the sun was bright. The daughter looked back, and her heart trembled. They passed the stone and the tree. At night they reached her father-in-law's house. The father-in-law stood in front and said: "Daughter, come in."
uncertain: póteys dʰugh₂tḗr: 'the master's daughter'
h₁íh₂m̥ h₁ím úd tl̥néh₂t: two accusatives; h₁ím (masc.) read as goal 'onto it (the wagon, kʷékʷlos)'
sh₂wéns kʷékʷlos: 'wheel of the sun' or 'the wagon was bright with/from the sun'
h₂ew spéḱyet: h₂ew 'away/back', 'looked back'
dʰgʷʰh₂ént: 'came near, passed by'
misfit: yéwgt: AOR 3sg, but the subject h₂néres 'men' is nom. pl.; a 3pl (yugént) is needed

english: The horses said: "Listen, sheep! Our heart aches when we see this: man, the master, makes the sheep's wool into a warm garment for himself, and the sheep have no wool."
uncertain: whole text: Schleicher-fable style without laryngeals or accents; analyzer cannot parse most tokens
widontbʰyos: dat. pl. ptcp. 'to (us) seeing'; no pronoun 'us' stated
kʷr̥neti soi: 'makes for himself'
misfit: eḱwos: written as nom. sg. (short o; this text marks vowel length elsewhere, e.g. owiyōm), but the verb wewekur is 3pl; nom. pl. eḱwōs is needed (the text is outside the corpus's laryngeal notation)

english: Two brothers lived together. The two wives drew water from the river. Their husbands were working; the sun was burning. One brother's wife said to the other's wife: "You deceived me." She said: "I did not deceive you." Then the words ran to the husbands. One brother struck the other, and blood came out. The two women cried out, and the father-in-law heard. He arrived and stood between them. "Let go (of each other), you two! What have you done?" Distress filled the household. The two stood and looked down.
uncertain: wékʷesh₂ ... drémt: neuter pl. subject with sg. verb (regular); 'the words (the quarrel) reached the husbands'
l̥h₁tóm: AOR/IMP 2du of 'let go'; 'stop!'
ḱóymom: adj. 'of the family' used as 'household'
sth₂éh₁yetām ... spéḱyetām: 3du; taken as the two brothers (could be the two women)
póteyes wr̥ǵyónt / pótins: the two husbands are plural, while the rest of the text uses the dual; they agree with each other, so this is not a misfit

english: When a son is born to a man, his friends come to his home bringing gifts. The shepherd brings a ram, the cook cooks it for the guests, a woman brings honey, the smith makes a gift, the carpenter builds a yoke for him, the master of the house gives them mead, and they drink and eat. Whoever brings a gift, the master gives him a gift in return. The friends are many, and the child grows.
uncertain: ḱéywōs: adj. 'intimate, dear', used as noun 'friends, kin'
h₁ésmey (yoke for him): referent ambiguous, the newborn or the father
déh₃reh₂ / dóh₃r̥ / déh₃nom / déh₃rom: four different 'gift' words
gʷḗn: analyzer gives VOC/LEMMA; taken as nom. sg.
misfit: ǵónh₁oh₁: instr. sg. / nom. du., used as subject of 3sg bʰuHyéti 'grows'; nom. sg. ǵónh₁os is needed (unless read impersonally 'it grows with offspring')

english: A brother is a fortress to a brother. A deceitful tongue splits brothers. The tongue is a snake. An old man's word is a path. A mother's heart is a fire. A good father-in-law is fire in winter. A good daughter-in-law is honey. A brother-in-law of bad fame is a worm in the apple. The woman who deceives her husband is a wolf in the house. The deceiver has honey on his tongue and a snake in his heart. A wolf does not become a dog. Two brothers pull the wagon in one yoke. Where brothers sit together, there a fire burns. This is an old saying.
uncertain: bʰérǵʰs: 'something high and fortified'; 'fortress'
dusḱléwēs: compound dus- 'bad' + ḱléwos 'fame', not analyzed; 'ill-famed'
h₁ésyeh₂s pótim: anaphoric 'her', not reflexive swóm; taken as her own husband
kʷór: lexicon 'where?; somewhere'; used here as relative 'where', with h₂én 'there' after it
yugóy: loc. sg. 'in the yoke' (or du.)
wékʷos: 'word', here 'saying'

english: The horses then said: "Listen, sheep! Our heart aches when we see this: man, the master, makes the sheep's wool into a warm garment for himself, and the sheep have no wool."
uncertain: whole text: Schleicher's 1868 a-vocalism spelling (akwāsas, wawakant, kard, agʰnutai), not this corpus's laryngeal notation; no token analyzes; translated by comparison with the same fable
ā: particle, 'then'
wiwidwant-swas: perfect ptcp. 'having seen' + reflexive 'we ourselves'; segmentation uncertain

english: What does a mortal carry? It is not on his shoulder. His father gave it to him at birth. Mortals speak it. A man hears it. No one eats it, no one drinks it. Fire does not burn it, water does not carry it away. When the man lies in the earth, it lives. What is it? It is the name.
uncertain: ǵn̥h₁téy: loc. of ǵénh₁tis 'birth', 'at birth'
dʰéh₁t: 'put, placed'; rendered 'gave' (with dat. h₁ésmey)
ḱléwseti: 'listens'; 'hears it'

english: Two brothers stood before the father. He listened to the two, and then he said: "Whoever struck his own brother, let him give a ram to the other. And she who deceived, let her carry water for the other's wife." Then the two heard his word. That one led a ram to him, and she carried water. Then the old man said: "Sit down, you two, and drink wine. A brother's blood is not water." The two sat down and drank.
uncertain: ph₂téri: loc. 'at/beside the father'
h₁yéh₂ ... séh₂: fem. 'she who', implying one of the wives; no woman is introduced beforehand
só moysóm h₁ím wédʰet: two accusatives; h₁ím read as goal 'to him (the other brother)'
nu-kʷe: 'and then'

english: It was growing dark. The night turned cold. The shepherd's wife lay in the house, and her husband kept watch. Then dawn shone, the sky turned red, and a son came forth. He cried. Then the father saw him, and his heart rejoiced. Then the father showed him the sun, gave him a famous name, and said: "May you live many years; may your name not die; may your fame be imperishable." Then the mother heard him and said: "He is dear to us; may he grow and become strong."
uncertain: h₁regʷesyét: impersonal, no subject
bʰéwdʰet: 'was awake, watchful'
swóm-kʷe ḱḗr: reflexive 'his own heart' (nom. n.)
sóh₂wl̥ woydéyet: causative 'made (him) see the sun' = showed him the sun
h₁ím ḱléwt (mother): 'him' = the father speaking

english: Father, go by the path, go by the path of the fathers. Cross the river by boat; may the boat carry him. Dawn, daughter of the sky, shine for him. Sun, look upon him. Earth, mother, receive him. May he sit with the fathers; may he drink poured mead. May his name not die. May his fame be imperishable. We remember him.
uncertain: déh₂nu nh₂éwh₁ gʷh₂dʰí: 'go (across) the river by boat'; déh₂nu acc./loc.
h₁ím / h₁ésmey: 3rd person 'him' right after the father was addressed as 'you'; the prayer turns from the dead man to the gods
sóh₂wl̥: nom./voc. same form; vocative here
memn̥mé: PRF 1pl 'we remember'

english: A man and a master sat down together. The master said: "I give you my daughter. Give me your pledge." The two gave pledges. Then the man said: "The Sky hears, and Mother Earth hears. The sun has seen it and the river knows it. Whoever breaks this pledge, may his cattle perish, may his name die." Then the two drank wine, and night came.
uncertain: h₁íh₂m̥: fem. 'it', referring to the pledge (bʰoydʰéh₂, fem.)
dʰéǵʰōm-kʷe méh₂tēr: 'and Mother Earth' (or 'Earth and Mother')
pótis: 'master, lord' (the girl's father)
Hrunépeti: SBJV 'breaks / should break'

english: A woman came to her husband at night and said: "Hear me. Your brother spoke to me. He said: 'In our house you are a stranger. You eat our honey and our butter.' I am not a stranger; I am your wife." He listened to her and said: "He said this? He said that? I will go to my brother and speak to him. In this home you are not a stranger; you are dear to me." Then he stood up and went to him. He found him with the horses and spoke to him.
uncertain: gʰóstis: 'guest / stranger'
ḱód wéwket? h₁íd wéwket: 'this' vs. 'that/it'; the second could be the wife's answer 'He said it'
h₁éḱwōys: instr. pl. 'with/among the horses'
h₁r̥sḱṓh₂: SBJV 1sg 'I will go to'
misfit: nos nos: the enclitic 'our' is written twice in a row (mélit nos nos h₃éngʷn̥-kʷe); one copy is extra, or the second belongs after h₃éngʷn̥
